wave_height_definition: NDBC WVHT, significant wave height, converted from metres on an exact 'm' unit-string match

_schema.default_swell_ceiling_ft: Significant wave height above which a reef window is called off regardless of tide. Applies to every spot with no override.
_schema.confidence: uncalibrated = author estimate, never field-checked, not safe to present as a threshold anyone should trust. calibrated = confirmed by someone who goes there. No value in this file is calibrated yet.

_provenance: PROVENANCE CLASS 2: AUTHOR ESTIMATE, and CORRIDOR-WIDE. What is left in this file after 0.2.0 is the value that applies to every spot with nothing said about it specifically. Anything that is a judgement about ONE activity or ONE spot has gone to the activity that owns it: the two per-spot swell overrides are in activities/surf/thresholds.json, and tidepool's minimum useful window is a constant in activities/tidepool/policy.ts. The old paragraph here explained only why this file is not spots.json, which stopped being the interesting question once the file split -- the interesting question is why a value is corridor-wide rather than an activity's, and the answer for the default ceiling is that every spot the grid renders uses it and no spot record justifies moving it. It is still not joined against any upstream authority, which is still why it is not in spots.json. See docs/adr/0012-threshold-is-a-role-and-author-estimate-is-a-provenance-class.md.
unresolved: Every one of the 8 spots the grid does render uses default_swell_ceiling_ft. No per-spot swell calibration exists for any of them. The UI must disclose the ceiling as uncalibrated wherever it drives a veto.

3.0 ft is an author estimate of when a reef shelf stops being workable, not a measured figure. It is one number standing in for eight reefs with different exposure, orientation and shelf depth. Sunset Cliffs is the spot where being wrong matters most: spots.json already flags it as a ledge system with cliff access where a wrong floor strands people, and the same is true of a wrong ceiling.

Significant wave height at an offshore or nearshore buoy is not breaking height at the reef. No shoaling or refraction transform is applied. The ceiling is calibrated against the buoy number as reported, which is the only thing the stack actually measures.
